retrieval_candidates.document: Slide 7: Why Standard Transformers Are Not Enough Here's where we hit a real technical problem. Standard attention, the method used in regular transformers, works by comparing every single position in a sequence to every other position. That means if you double how long your sequence is, the amount of computer work goes up by four times, not two times — that's what's called quadratic growth, versus the much gentler, near-linear growth we want instead. That's fine for the sequence lengths normal language models deal with, usually a few thousand up to maybe a hundred thousand tokens. But it becomes completely unworkable once you're talking about a million tokens, especially when you're training a huge model on trillions of examples. And this really matters in biology, because the parts of DNA that control genes, and the connections between genes, can be spread hundreds of thousands, even millions, of letters apart. So if you want to catch these long-distance relationships, you genuinely need a model that can look across that much space at once — you can't just fake it with a clever shortcut. Put those two facts together, and you get the conclusion: at the level of looking at every single DNA letter, with a goal of a 1 million letter view, regular attention is simply too expensive to train, no matter how much computer hardware you have. This is actually the same wall that a lot of AI researchers have been running into with long text sequences too, which is why people have already built things like sparse attention, other efficient attention tricks, and convolution-based models like the earlier version of Hyena. Evo 2 builds on that same line of work, but has to push it even further, because DNA doesn't give you an easy shortcut the way language does — you really do need to look at every single letter, one at a time. So here's the real question: can we build a model whose cost grows slowly and gently as the sequence gets longer, while still being able to catch those important long-distance patterns, the way attention can? That answer is the single most important idea in this whole talk, and it's what we're covering next. Slide 8: This is the most important part of the talk, so let's take our time. Evo 2 uses a hybrid design made up of four repeating components that are stacked together to build the full model. Three of these are called SE, MR, and LI, which are different types of Hyena operators, and the fourth is a small amount of regular attention. SE, or Short Explicit Hyena, handles patterns that are close together in the sequence, like the three-letter codons we talked about earlier. MR, or Medium Regularized Hyena, handles patterns that are a bit farther apart. LI, or Long Implicit Hyena, is responsible for finding patterns over very long distances. Researchers can improve the accuracy further by adding a small classifier, called a probe, on top of the model. This method is especially useful for difficult mutations outside genes, for important genes like BRCA1, and it works across many different species because Evo 2 was trained on DNA from across the tree of life. Slide 11: Generating DNA: Biological Design Evo 2's second big skill flips the same mechanism around. Because it was trained to always guess the next letter, you can also just run it forward instead of only using it to score existing sequences. You start with some beginning sequence, or even nothing at all, and you pick one letter at a time based on what the model thinks is likely to come next. Then you feed that chosen letter back in as new context, and repeat the whole process again and again. This is exactly the same idea used to generate text with a chatbot — the only real difference is you're working with four possible letters instead of a huge vocabulary of words, and "making sense" here means looking like real, working DNA instead of a coherent sentence. According to the paper, sequences created this way make sense not just letter by letter, but across the whole sequence, at the scale of an entire genome. That means Evo 2 can generate DNA that looks like it could belong to real mitochondria — a small structure inside cells — real bacteria, and even more complex organisms, and by several measurements, these generated sequences look more natural and realistic than ones made by earlier methods. But just picking letters at random only gets you "some" believable sequence. For real design work, scientists usually want a sequence with a specific goal in mind, like a particular structure related to how DNA gets packaged and controlled inside a cell. That's where guided search comes in: instead of retraining the whole model for every new goal, you steer the letter-picking process itself while it's happening, checking and adjusting partial sequences as they're being built, to push them toward the property you actually want. If that reminds you of guided or constrained text generation in language models, where you steer the output toward a certain style or rule without retraining anything, that's exactly the same idea, just applied to DNA. The paper says this is the first time anyone has shown that spending more computer effort on this guided search, at the moment of generating, actually leads to better results in biology — which is similar to a trend you may have seen in language and reasoning AI models recently, where doing more "thinking" at answer time improves the output. retrieval_candidates.document: Slide 15: Why Evo 2 Matters Let's bring this full circle back to where we started. This is one single trained model, used without any extra training, for both prediction and generation, across every branch of life — not a bunch of separate specialized models. It runs on an architecture that actually scales: StripedHyena 2 is the reason a million-letter view at full detail is even possible, something a regular transformer just couldn't manage. It was also released fully open — the trained model, the code, and the entire 9.3 trillion letter OpenGenome2 dataset were all made freely available, which is a big part of why so much follow-up research already exists on this model in such a short time. And maybe most interesting of all, the model figured out real biology on its own: patterns like gene boundaries and control switches showed up on their own, with zero labels involved, purely as a side effect of the model trying to guess the next DNA letter — the exact same thing we've seen happen again and again with language models, just now shown in a completely different area, biology. I want to leave you with this thought: if GPT learned the language written by people, Evo 2 is learning the language written by four billion years of evolution. I want to be clear that this isn't a settled fact — it's really an open question the field is still working through. Whether genomic models will actually keep improving the same way language models have, and how far this comparison really holds up, is something researchers are still actively figuring out.

retrieval_candidates.document: Slide 13: Limitations No model is perfect, and Evo 2 has some important limitations. First, everything it produces—whether it's a harmfulness score or a newly generated DNA sequence—is only a prediction, not a medical decision. Any result that could affect patient care must still be tested in a laboratory or confirmed through clinical studies before anyone acts on it. Second, because Evo 2 can generate realistic DNA sequences, there's a genuine concern about misuse. The same technology that can be used for helpful applications in synthetic biology could also be misused. To reduce this risk, the researchers excluded viruses that infect plants, animals, and humans from the training data, making it harder for the model to help generate something dangerous. This is an important safety measure, but it doesn't eliminate all the risks, especially since the model is fully open. Another limitation is the amount of computing power needed to train a model like this. Training required over 1,000 GPUs and trillions of DNA letters, making it unrealistic for most universities or research labs to build a similar model from scratch. Finally, Evo 2 doesn't perform equally well on every type of gene or mutation. Independent studies found that its accuracy varies depending on the task, and some datasets contain far more harmless mutations than harmful ones, which can make the overall score look better than the model's performance on the rarer, more important cases. This reminds us that we should always look beyond a single accuracy score when evaluating an AI model. Now that we've covered both the strengths and limitations, let's look at where this research could go in the future. Slide 14: Future Directions The paper also discusses where models like Evo 2 could be useful in the future. In drug discovery, it can help researchers identify which mutations are worth testing, saving time and money. Because DNA contains the instructions for making proteins, Evo 2 could also support protein engineering by helping design DNA that produces proteins with useful properties. In synthetic biology, future versions may even help design entire genomes instead of just small DNA sequences. Another exciting application is personalized medicine, where the model could predict whether a person's unique genetic variants are likely to be harmful. Beyond biology, the StripedHyena 2 architecture could also benefit AI systems that need to process very long sequences, such as long documents, codebases, or videos. Looking further ahead, researchers also hope to build models that learn from DNA, RNA, and proteins together for a more complete understanding of biology

retrieval_candidates.document: Slide 7: Why Standard Transformers Are Not Enough Here's where we hit a real technical problem. Standard attention, the method used in regular transformers, works by comparing every single position in a sequence to every other position. That means if you double how long your sequence is, the amount of computer work goes up by four times, not two times — that's what's called quadratic growth, versus the much gentler, near-linear growth we want instead. That's fine for the sequence lengths normal language models deal with, usually a few thousand up to maybe a hundred thousand tokens. But it becomes completely unworkable once you're talking about a million tokens, especially when you're training a huge model on trillions of examples. And this really matters in biology, because the parts of DNA that control genes, and the connections between genes, can be spread hundreds of thousands, even millions, of letters apart. So if you want to catch these long-distance relationships, you genuinely need a model that can look across that much space at once — you can't just fake it with a clever shortcut. Put those two facts together, and you get the conclusion: at the level of looking at every single DNA letter, with a goal of a 1 million letter view, regular attention is simply too expensive to train, no matter how much computer hardware you have. This is actually the same wall that a lot of AI researchers have been running into with long text sequences too, which is why people have already built things like sparse attention, other efficient attention tricks, and convolution-based models like the earlier version of Hyena. Evo 2 builds on that same line of work, but has to push it even further, because DNA doesn't give you an easy shortcut the way language does — you really do need to look at every single letter, one at a time. So here's the real question: can we build a model whose cost grows slowly and gently as the sequence gets longer, while still being able to catch those important long-distance patterns, the way attention can? retrieval_candidates.document: Slide 13: Limitations No model is perfect, and Evo 2 has some important limitations. First, everything it produces—whether it's a harmfulness score or a newly generated DNA sequence—is only a prediction, not a medical decision. Any result that could affect patient care must still be tested in a laboratory or confirmed through clinical studies before anyone acts on it. Second, because Evo 2 can generate realistic DNA sequences, there's a genuine concern about misuse. The same technology that can be used for helpful applications in synthetic biology could also be misused. To reduce this risk, the researchers excluded viruses that infect plants, animals, and humans from the training data, making it harder for the model to help generate something dangerous. This is an important safety measure, but it doesn't eliminate all the risks, especially since the model is fully open. Another limitation is the amount of computing power needed to train a model like this. Training required over 1,000 GPUs and trillions of DNA letters, making it unrealistic for most universities or research labs to build a similar model from scratch. Finally, Evo 2 doesn't perform equally well on every type of gene or mutation. Independent studies found that its accuracy varies depending on the task, and some datasets contain far more harmless mutations than harmful ones, which can make the overall score look better than the model's performance on the rarer, more important cases. This reminds us that we should always look beyond a single accuracy score when evaluating an AI model. Now that we've covered both the strengths and limitations, let's look at where this research could go in the future. Slide 14: Future Directions The paper also discusses where models like Evo 2 could be useful in the future. In drug discovery, it can help researchers identify which mutations are worth testing, saving time and money. Because DNA contains the instructions for making proteins, Evo 2 could also support protein engineering by helping design DNA that produces proteins with useful properties. In synthetic biology, future versions may even help design entire genomes instead of just small DNA sequences. Another exciting application is personalized medicine, where the model could predict whether a person's unique genetic variants are likely to be harmful. Beyond biology, the StripedHyena 2 architecture could also benefit AI systems that need to process very long sequences, such as long documents, codebases, or videos. Looking further ahead, researchers also hope to build models that learn from DNA, RNA, and proteins together for a more complete understanding of biology

retrieval_candidates.document: Slide 15: Why Evo 2 Matters Let's bring this full circle back to where we started. This is one single trained model, used without any extra training, for both prediction and generation, across every branch of life — not a bunch of separate specialized models. It runs on an architecture that actually scales: StripedHyena 2 is the reason a million-letter view at full detail is even possible, something a regular transformer just couldn't manage. It was also released fully open — the trained model, the code, and the entire 9.3 trillion letter OpenGenome2 dataset were all made freely available, which is a big part of why so much follow-up research already exists on this model in such a short time. And maybe most interesting of all, the model figured out real biology on its own: patterns like gene boundaries and control switches showed up on their own, with zero labels involved, purely as a side effect of the model trying to guess the next DNA letter — the exact same thing we've seen happen again and again with language models, just now shown in a completely different area, biology. I want to leave you with this thought: if GPT learned the language written by people, Evo 2 is learning the language written by four billion years of evolution. I want to be clear that this isn't a settled fact — it's really an open question the field is still working through. Whether genomic models will actually keep improving the same way language models have, and how far this comparison really holds up, is something researchers are still actively figuring out.

Standard attention, the method used in regular transformers, works by comparing every single position in a sequence to every other position. That means if you double how long your sequence is, the amount of computer work goes up by four times, not two times — that's what's called quadratic growth, versus the much gentler, near-linear growth we want instead. That's fine for the sequence lengths normal language models deal with, usually a few thousand up to maybe a hundred thousand tokens. But it becomes completely unworkable once you're talking about a million tokens, especially when you're training a huge model on trillions of examples. And this really matters in biology, because the parts of DNA that control genes, and the connections between genes, can be spread hundreds of thousands, even millions, of letters apart. So if you want to catch these long-distance relationships, you genuinely need a model that can look across that much space at once — you can't just fake it with a clever shortcut. Put those two facts together, and you get the conclusion: at the level of looking at every single DNA letter, with a goal of a 1 million letter view, regular attention is simply too expensive to train, no matter how much computer hardware you have. This is actually the same wall that a lot of AI researchers have been running into with long text sequences too, which is why people have already built things like sparse attention, other efficient attention tricks, and convolution-based models like the earlier version of Hyena. Evo 2 builds on that same line of work, but has to push it even further, because DNA doesn't give you an easy shortcut the way language does — you really do need to look at every single letter, one at a time. That string gets broken into tokens, one letter at a time. Remember, a token is just one small piece the model reads at a time. Unlike some language models, which group several letters together into one token, here every single DNA letter gets its own token — nothing gets squeezed together or simplified. The model then predicts the next letter, and that prediction gets compared to what the real next letter actually was, using something called cross-entropy loss, which is just a math way of measuring how wrong or right a guess was — it's the exact same method used to train language models. This process repeats at every single position in the genome, over and over, trillions of times, and the model is never told what a gene is or what a mutation is. It only ever tries to guess the next letter. Why does this actually work? First, no labels are needed. The correct answer here is simply whatever letter actually comes next in a real DNA sequence — and that's available in unlimited amounts, with zero human work needed to label it. Compare that to trying to build a list of "these mutations are harmful, these are not" by hand, which would take forever. Second, this forces the model to learn useful patterns along the way. retrieval_candidates.document: Slide 13: Limitations No model is perfect, and Evo 2 has some important limitations. First, everything it produces—whether it's a harmfulness score or a newly generated DNA sequence—is only a prediction, not a medical decision. Any result that could affect patient care must still be tested in a laboratory or confirmed through clinical studies before anyone acts on it. Second, because Evo 2 can generate realistic DNA sequences, there's a genuine concern about misuse. The same technology that can be used for helpful applications in synthetic biology could also be misused. To reduce this risk, the researchers excluded viruses that infect plants, animals, and humans from the training data, making it harder for the model to help generate something dangerous. This is an important safety measure, but it doesn't eliminate all the risks, especially since the model is fully open. Another limitation is the amount of computing power needed to train a model like this. Training required over 1,000 GPUs and trillions of DNA letters, making it unrealistic for most universities or research labs to build a similar model from scratch. Finally, Evo 2 doesn't perform equally well on every type of gene or mutation. Independent studies found that its accuracy varies depending on the task, and some datasets contain far more harmless mutations than harmful ones, which can make the overall score look better than the model's performance on the rarer, more important cases. This reminds us that we should always look beyond a single accuracy score when evaluating an AI model. Now that we've covered both the strengths and limitations, let's look at where this research could go in the future. Slide 14: Future Directions The paper also discusses where models like Evo 2 could be useful in the future. In drug discovery, it can help researchers identify which mutations are worth testing, saving time and money. Because DNA contains the instructions for making proteins, Evo 2 could also support protein engineering by helping design DNA that produces proteins with useful properties. In synthetic biology, future versions may even help design entire genomes instead of just small DNA sequences. Another exciting application is personalized medicine, where the model could predict whether a person's unique genetic variants are likely to be harmful. Beyond biology, the StripedHyena 2 architecture could also benefit AI systems that need to process very long sequences, such as long documents, codebases, or videos. Looking further ahead, researchers also hope to build models that learn from DNA, RNA, and proteins together for a more complete understanding of biology

Slide 2: The Evolution of Foundation Models To answer that, it helps to walk through how AI got here in the first place. In the early days, AI was task-specific. That means one model did one job. You'd build a separate model for spotting spam, another one for translating language, another one for recognizing pictures. Each of these needed its own labeled data, made carefully by hand. Then GPT changed the game. Instead of building a new model for every job, you train one big model with a very simple goal: guess the next word. You train it on huge amounts of raw text that nobody had to label by hand, and that one model turns out to be useful for many different tasks afterward, without needing to be rebuilt each time. Vision models did something similar with images, learning straight from raw pixels. Then multimodal models combined text, images, and audio into one shared model. Notice the pattern here: at each step, the model gets more general, the training data gets less carefully labeled, and the model has to figure out more on its own. Slide 3: Understanding DNA as Information Let's cover some quick biology, and I'll tie it straight back to AI ideas you already know. DNA is built from four basic building blocks, called bases: A, T, G, and C, standing for Adenine, Thymine, Guanine, and Cytosine. That's really it. That is the entire "alphabet" that all life is written in. A genome is just the full DNA sequence of a living thing. It's basically a very long string made only from these four letters — from a few million letters for a simple bacteria, to over three billion letters for a human. Here's the important part for this audience: one single DNA letter can be treated just like a token in a language model. If you remember, a token is just a small piece of text, like a word or part of a word, that a language model reads one at a time. In DNA, each letter is one token. Its meaning depends on the letters around it, and in theory, you could predict it just from its surroundings, the same way a language model predicts the next word in a sentence. A gene is a piece of the DNA sequence that actually does something useful, kind of like one meaningful sentence hiding inside a very long, mostly boring document. A mutation is just a small change to that string — one letter gets swapped, added, or removed. And just like changing one word in a contract can totally change its meaning, changing one DNA letter in the right spot can break how a gene works, while changing a letter in another spot might do almost nothing. This is really the whole point I want you to take from this: order matters, just like word order matters in a sentence; one small change can flip the meaning completely, just like a typo can change what a sentence means; and sequence models — transformers, Hyena, or older models like RNNs — were built exactly to handle this kind of problem, predicting one symbol from the symbols around it. So the reason we can even try to use AI sequence models on DNA comes down to this: DNA is a string of symbols where order matters and small changes matter a lot, and that is exactly the kind of problem modern AI models are good at solving.
